usage: The standard pharmacy request; add 한 통 for a whole box or 한 알 for a single tablet
Oral meds always pair with 먹다, never 마시다 even though English says 'take'
센 is the natural everyday adjective for potency here; 강한 sounds stiff and technical
효과가 있다 = it works; 효과가 빠르다 = it kicks in fast
examples: 진통제 한 알 주세요.
Please give me one painkiller.
Simplest counter form: 한 알 = one tablet, with 알 the counter for pills
머리가 너무 아픈데 진통제 있어요?
My head hurts so much, do you have any painkillers?
Everyday opener at a 약국; -은데 softly sets up the request
생리통이 심해서 진통제 두 알 먹었는데도 안 나아요.
My cramps are bad so I took two painkillers but it's still not better.
Real-situation: -는데도 = 'even though'; 안 나아요 = doesn't get better
nuance: 진통제 is the everyday word for any pain-relief pill — headache, cramps, muscle ache — and a pharmacist understands it instantly. The hanja is 鎭痛劑 'suppress-pain-agent': 鎭 calm/suppress, 痛 pain, 劑 a prepared dose, the same 劑 that marks 해열제 and 소화제. The dividing line you must learn is 진통제 (relieves the pain itself) versus 해열제 (lowers a fever); many products do both, but the words name different jobs, so don't treat them as synonyms. Register is fully neutral — kids, grandparents and pharmacists all use it — though in casual speech people often just say the brand 타이레놀. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the verb: English 'take a pill' tempts learners into 마시다 or even 가지다, but a pill is always 먹다 (literally 'eat'), and you count it with 알, not 개.

Counting with 개: it should be 진통제 한 알, because 알 is the counter for tablets

usage: Please give me some digestive medicine
The go-to request after a heavy meal
먹다 covers both the chewable tablets and the liquid bottles colloquially
I bought digestive medicine because I couldn't digest
소화가 안 되다 = to have indigestion, the most natural framing
a digestive medicine like Gas Hwalmyeongsu
Names the famous liquid 소화제 brand pharmacists will recognize
examples: 소화제 하나 주세요.
Please give me one digestive medicine.
Simple counter: 하나 / 한 개 works for a bottle or sachet
과식해서 소화제 먹고 누웠어요.
I overate so I took digestive medicine and lay down.
Everyday cause-result: 과식하다 = to overeat
체했는데 소화제 먹어도 속이 계속 더부룩해요.
I have an upset stomach and even after digestive medicine my belly still feels bloated.
Real-situation: 체하다 = stomach 'blocked'; 더부룩하다 = bloated, the signature 소화제 symptom
nuance: 소화제 is what you ask for after eating too much or when you feel 체했어요 (food 'stuck'), and it covers both chewable tablets and the popular liquid bottles like 까스활명수. The hanja is 消化劑 'dissolve-transform-agent': 消 to dissolve/dispel, 化 to change, 劑 a prepared dose — literally an 'agent that makes food break down'. The sharp contrast to memorize is 소화제 versus 위장약: 소화제 is narrowly for digestion after overeating, while 위장약 is the broader stomach medicine for acid, burning (속쓰림) and gastritis. The register is neutral and all-ages. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, learners invent 소화약 by analogy with 감기약, but the correct, fixed form is 소화제 with the Sino-Korean -제 suffix; second, don't reach for 마시다 just because the liquid type is a drink — Koreans still say 소화제 먹다.

Using 마시다 for the liquid bottle — even drinkable 소화제 pairs with 먹다 in normal speech

usage: Please give me a fever reducer
The standard pharmacy request when running a fever
to give a fever reducer (to someone)
먹이다 is the causative 'to feed/administer', used for a child or patient
I had a fever so I took a fever reducer
열이 나다 = to run a fever, the set phrase
-용 (用) = 'for the use of'; ask this way for kids' doses
examples: 해열제 좀 주세요.
Please give me a fever reducer.
Simplest request; 좀 softens it politely
열이 38도가 넘어서 해열제 먹었어요.
My fever was over 38 degrees so I took a fever reducer.
Everyday: Koreans cite 도 (Celsius degrees) for fever
아이한테 해열제 먹였는데도 열이 안 떨어져요.
Even after I gave my child a fever reducer the fever won't come down.
Real-situation: -한테 먹이다 = give meds to someone; 열이 떨어지다 = the fever drops
nuance: 해열제 is the go-to word when 열이 나요 (you have a fever), and pharmacists grasp it at once. The hanja is 解熱劑 'release-heat-agent': 解 to loosen/release, 熱 heat/fever, 劑 a dose — so literally 'an agent that releases the body's heat'. The contrast to fix in your mind is 해열제 versus 감기약: 해열제 does one job, dropping a fever, while 감기약 is the umbrella cold remedy that bundles fever, runny nose and cough together; they overlap but are not the same word. Register is neutral, used at home and in clinics alike. A key pitfall is the verb shift when you dose someone else: you 먹다 medicine yourself, but you 먹이다 (causative) it to a child — English uses 'give' for both, so learners wrongly say 해열제 줬어요 when they mean they administered it. Also resist inventing 열약; the fixed term is 해열제.

mistakes: Saying 열약 — the correct, fixed term is 해열제 (解熱劑)

Using 해열제 줬어요 to mean you dosed a child — administering meds to someone is 먹이다 (먹였어요), not just 주다

usage: Please give me some cold medicine
The single most common pharmacy request for newcomers
먹다 covers both pills and the liquid sachets
Name your main symptom: 콧물 (runny nose) / 기침 (cough) / 목 (throat)
Pharmacists ask 졸린 거 vs 안 졸린 거 — drowsy vs non-drowsy
examples: 감기약 주세요.
Please give me cold medicine.
Simplest form; just name the product so the pharmacist knows what you need
감기 기운이 있어서 감기약 사러 왔어요.
I'm coming down with a cold so I came to buy cold medicine.
Everyday: 감기 기운 = the onset/feeling of a cold, a very natural phrase
일해야 해서 안 졸린 감기약으로 주세요.
I have to work, so please give me the non-drowsy cold medicine.
Real-situation: -(으)로 주세요 = 'give me the one that is...', specifying a variant
nuance: 감기약 is the umbrella term for cold remedies and the single most common thing a newcomer buys at a 약국. Note the formation: 감기 is Sino-Korean 感氣 'catch-air/energy' (the Korean concept of a cold as bad air entering the body), but the medicine takes the native suffix -약 ('medicine'), not the Sino-Korean -제 you see in 진통제·해열제·소화제 — so it is 감기약, never 감기제. The contrast worth knowing is 감기약 versus 해열제: 감기약 bundles several cold symptoms (fever, runny nose, cough) into one product, while 해열제 targets fever alone. Register is completely neutral and essential daily vocabulary. The pitfall: English speakers walk in and ask only for 약 ('medicine'), which tells the pharmacist nothing — always say 감기약 — and they forget that 감기약 varies a lot by symptom, so be ready to name 콧물, 기침 or 목.

usage: For cuts, burns, rashes and bites
바르다 'to spread/smear' is the fixed verb for creams and ointments
I put ointment on the wound
The spot takes the particle 에: 상처에 바르다
Name the target: 무좀 (athlete's foot), 안연고 (eye ointment)
examples: 여기 연고 좀 발라 주세요.
Please put some ointment on here.
Simple request; 발라 주세요 = please apply it (for me)
이 연고는 하루에 세 번 바르세요.
Apply this ointment three times a day.
Everyday dosage phrasing: 하루에 세 번 = three times a day
넘어져서 무릎 까졌는데 바르는 연고 있어요?
I fell and scraped my knee — do you have an ointment to put on it?
Real-situation: 까지다 = to get scraped; 바르는 연고 = the kind you apply
nuance: 연고 covers any medicated cream or salve for the skin — cuts, burns, bug bites, rashes — and is Sino-Korean 軟膏 'soft-paste': 軟 soft, 膏 ointment/grease, so literally 'a soft paste'. The verb is always 바르다 ('spread/smear onto'), which is the same verb you use for sunscreen, lotion and lip balm, and it is what cleanly separates 연고 from 파스 (a patch you 붙이다, stick on) and from oral medicine you 먹다. For a specific area, name it up front: 무좀 연고 (athlete's foot), 안연고 (eye ointment), 화상 연고 (burns). Register is neutral and everyday. The big English-speaker pitfall is treating ointment like a pill — 연고 먹다 is wrong because it is external only — and reaching for 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', used for walls and nails) instead of the correct 바르다 for putting medicine on skin.

Using 칠하다 (paint a surface) instead of 바르다 — medicine and cosmetics on skin always take 바르다
Marking the spot with the wrong particle — it's 상처에 연고를 바르다 (에 for the location), not 상처를

usage: Please give me a pain patch
For sore muscles and stiff shoulders
to stick on a pain patch
붙이다 'to stick/attach' is the verb for patches
I put a patch on my shoulder
The body part takes 에: 어깨에 붙이다
뿌리다 = to spray; the aerosol type of 파스
examples: 여기 파스 하나 붙여 주세요.
Please stick a patch on here.
Simple request; 하나 = one, 붙여 주세요 = please attach it
운동하고 나서 종아리에 파스 붙였어요.
After working out I put a patch on my calf.
Everyday: -고 나서 = after doing; 종아리 = calf
어깨가 결려서 파스 붙였더니 한결 시원해요.
My shoulder was stiff so I put on a patch and it feels much better.
Real-situation: 결리다 = to feel stiff/cramped; 시원하다 here = a soothing, cooling relief
nuance: 파스 is the everyday word for the medicated patches Koreans slap on sore muscles, stiff necks and tired legs. Unlike the -제 and -약 medicines around it, 파스 is a loanword (from German/Dutch 'pasta'/pleister, via Japanese パス), so it has no hanja and no suffix — just the bare borrowed noun. The verb is 붙이다 ('stick on'), which is exactly what separates it from 연고 (a cream you 바르다, spread) and from any pill you 먹다. People habitually mention the strong menthol 냄새 (smell) and the 시원한 (cooling) feel. Register is casual and extremely common in daily life. The English-speaker pitfall is verb choice driven by the English word 'apply': learners say 파스 바르다, but a patch is stuck on with 붙이다 — only the cream or spray variants use 바르다 / 뿌리다 — and some try to swallow it like a pill, when 파스 is strictly external.

usage: 붙이다 'to stick' is the verb; the strip adheres to the skin
장 is the counter for flat, sheet-like items
방수 (防水) = waterproof, handy for showering
examples: 반창고 한 장만 주세요.
Please give me just one band-aid.
Simple request with the counter 장 and 만 (just/only)
손을 베어서 반창고 붙였어요.
I cut my hand so I put on a band-aid.
Everyday: (손을) 베다 = to cut oneself
물집이 잡혔는데 반창고 붙이는 게 낫겠죠?
I got a blister — it'd be better to put a band-aid on, right?
Real-situation: 물집(이) 잡히다 = to get a blister; -겠죠? seeks light agreement
nuance: 반창고 is the standard word for a small adhesive bandage, and is Sino-Korean 絆瘡膏 'bind-sore-paste' (絆 to bind/tie, 瘡 a sore/wound, 膏 paste) — a vivid old image of a sticky strip that binds a wound shut. In real life many Koreans just say the genericized brand 대일밴드 or simply 밴드, all meaning the same thing. The verb is 붙이다 (stick on) and you count them with 장 (the flat-sheet counter). The contrast you must hold is 반창고 versus 붕대: 반창고 is the small ready-made strip for everyday nicks, while 붕대 is the long gauze roll you 감다 (wind) around a sprain or large wound. Register is fully neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'apply a bandage' and saying 반창고 바르다 — a band-aid is stuck on with 붙이다, never spread — and mixing up the counter by saying 한 개 instead of the natural 한 장.

usage: 감다 'to wind/wrap around' is the dedicated verb
I wrapped a bandage around my ankle
The body part takes 에: 발목에 감다
풀다 = to undo/loosen, the natural opposite of 감다
examples: 붕대 좀 주세요.
Please give me a bandage.
Simplest request; 좀 softens it
발목을 삐어서 붕대로 감았어요.
I sprained my ankle so I wrapped it with a bandage.
Everyday: 발목을 삐다 = to sprain one's ankle; -(으)로 = with/using
붕대를 너무 꽉 감으면 피가 안 통해요.
If you wrap the bandage too tightly, blood won't circulate.
Real-situation: 꽉 = tightly; 피가 통하다 = blood circulates
nuance: 붕대 is the rolled gauze bandage you wind around a sprain or a larger wound, and is Sino-Korean 繃帶 'bind-band' (繃 to bind/stretch tight, 帶 a band/belt) — literally a 'binding band', which is exactly how it behaves. Its signature verb is 감다 ('wind/wrap around'), with 풀다 to undo it, and this is what cleanly separates 붕대 from 반창고: a 붕대 is the long roll you wrap (감다) around an ankle or wrist, while a 반창고 is the small ready-made strip you stick on (붙이다) for a paper-cut. Register is neutral and clinical-but-common. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'put on a bandage' tempts learners into 붕대 붙이다, but you wrap it with 감다, not stick it; and learners blur 붕대 with 반창고, asking for the wrong item — say 붕대 for big areas and sprains, 반창고 for tiny nicks.

usage: For cleaning a cut before dressing it
바르다 (spread on) or 닦다 (wipe) for putting it on a wound
I cleaned the wound with antiseptic
따갑다 = to sting/smart, the classic reaction
examples: 소독약 좀 주세요.
Please give me some antiseptic.
Simplest request at the pharmacy counter
상처에 소독약 먼저 바르고 연고 바르세요.
Put antiseptic on the wound first, then apply ointment.
Everyday wound-care order: 소독약 → 연고 → 반창고
넘어진 데를 소독약으로 닦으니까 엄청 따가워요.
When I wipe the spot where I fell with antiseptic, it really stings.
Real-situation: 데 = spot/place; -(으)니까 shows result; 따갑다 = to sting
nuance: 소독약 is the everyday term for a wound antiseptic such as 포비돈 (povidone-iodine) or 과산화수소 (hydrogen peroxide), and pharmacists know it on sight. It is built from Sino-Korean 消毒 'dispel-poison' (消 to dissolve/dispel, 毒 poison/germs) plus the native suffix -약, so literally 'germ-dispelling medicine'. There is a real distinction to learn between 소독약 and 소독제: in everyday speech 소독약 leans toward the liquid you put on a cut, while 소독제 is the broader 'disinfectant' for hands, surfaces and equipment — overlapping but not identical. You 바르다 or 닦다 it onto skin, and people reliably note that it 따가워요 (stings). Register is neutral and practical for any home first-aid kit. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like medicine you take: 소독약 먹다 is wrong because it is external-only, and beware confusing it with 소독제 for surfaces.

usage: Asking at a pharmacy or checking at home
The common digital ear-type; 이마 체온계 = forehead type
체온(體溫) = body temperature; the natural object of 재다
examples: 체온계 있어요?
Do you have a thermometer?
Simplest yes/no question at the counter
체온계로 열을 재 보니까 38.5도였어요.
When I took my temperature with the thermometer it was 38.5 degrees.
Everyday: 열을 재다 = to take a temperature; -아 보니까 = upon trying
아기는 귀에 대는 체온계가 재기 편해요.
For a baby, the ear thermometer is the easiest to measure with.
Real-situation: 귀에 대다 = to put against the ear; -기 편하다 = easy to (do)
nuance: 체온계 is specifically the device for measuring body temperature, built from Sino-Korean 體溫 'body-warmth' (體 body, 溫 warmth) plus 計 'measuring instrument' — the same 計 in 온도계 (thermometer for air/water), 시계 (clock) and 체중계 (scale). That shared 計 is exactly where the trap lies: 체온계 measures a body, while 온도계 measures the temperature of a room, the water or an oven — do not swap them. The verb pairing is 재다 ('measure'), used with 열을 재다 or 체온을 재다. Since COVID, digital, 귀 (ear) and 이마 (forehead) types are everywhere and any 약국 sells one. Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'read the thermometer' or 'check my temperature' lures learners into 보다 ('look') or 읽다 ('read'), but Korean uses 재다 ('measure') — you 열을 재다, not 열을 보다 — and learners reach for the generic 온도계 when they need the body-specific 체온계.

usage: Please give me some stomach medicine
For stomach pain, acid or gastritis
먹다 for tablets and sachets alike
My stomach was burning so I took stomach medicine
속이 쓰리다 = to have a burning/sour stomach
stomach medicine on an empty stomach
빈속 = empty stomach; note dosing timing matters
examples: 위장약 좀 주세요.
Please give me some stomach medicine.
Simplest counter request; 좀 softens it
요즘 속이 자주 쓰려서 위장약 먹고 있어요.
These days my stomach often burns, so I'm taking stomach medicine.
Everyday chronic-complaint phrasing with -고 있다
술 마시기 전에 위장약 미리 먹는 사람도 많아요.
Lots of people take stomach medicine in advance before drinking.
Real-situation: 미리 = in advance; reflects Korean drinking culture
nuance: 위장약 is the broad term for stomach and gut medicine, covering acid, burning (속쓰림), bloating and gastritis. It is Sino-Korean 胃腸 'stomach-intestines' (胃 stomach, 腸 intestines) plus native -약, so literally 'stomach-and-gut medicine' — the wider scope is right there in the two organs named. The contrast you must keep straight is 위장약 versus 소화제: 위장약 treats pain, acid and burning across the digestive tract, whereas 소화제 is the narrow remedy for when food won't go down after overeating. A pharmacist will ask your exact symptom — 속쓰림 (burning), 더부룩함 (bloating), 통증 (pain) — before choosing. Register is neutral and very practical for adults in Korea. The English-speaker pitfall is using 위장약 and 소화제 as if interchangeable, and inventing the clipped 위약 (which actually means 'placebo', 僞藥!) — the correct word is the full 위장약.

usage: A common reason to ask for liquid or powder instead
알 is both the noun root and the counter for round small things
가루약 = powdered medicine; 말고 = not (that) but
삼키다 = to swallow, more precise than 먹다 here
examples: 알약 한 알 주세요.
Please give me one tablet.
Simplest form with the counter 알
이 알약은 하루에 두 알씩 드세요.
Take two of these tablets a day.
Everyday dosage: 두 알씩 = two each (per time); 씩 = per/apiece
저는 알약을 잘 못 삼켜서 물약으로 주실 수 있어요?
I can't really swallow pills, so could you give me the liquid form?
Real-situation: 물약 = liquid medicine; -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요? makes a polite request
nuance: 알약 is the everyday word for a solid pill or tablet, and it is a transparent native compound: 알 (a small round thing — a grain, an egg, a berry) + 약 (medicine), literally a 'pellet medicine'. That same 알 doubles as the counter, so you say 한 알, 두 알 — and using 개 here sounds unnatural. The three-way contrast to learn is 알약 (solid tablet) versus 가루약 (powder) versus 물약 (liquid); pharmacists offer these as alternatives. The verbs are 먹다 (general 'take') or, more precisely, 삼키다 ('swallow'). Register is neutral. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: the counter (it's 한 알, not 한 개), and word order — learners flip the compound into 약알, but the head noun comes last in Korean, so it must be 알약. If swallowing is hard, it's completely normal to ask for 물약 or 가루약.
